_comment: The full approvals path for an Alberta data centre, provincial through municipal, ending at occupancy. A MAP OF PROCESS, not legal advice: it shows who decides what, what must precede what, and what can run in parallel. Every node links to the body that runs it so a reader can start there. Durations are deliberately absent — they vary by project and queue position, and quoting one would be inventing a number.
title: From first enquiry to occupancy
intro: A data centre needs approvals from four different authorities on four different clocks. Most can run in parallel — and must, because the grid connection is almost always the long pole. This shows the whole path, what blocks what, and where each process is actually started.
caution: A map of the process, not legal advice. Confirm each requirement against the authority named before relying on it.

lanes.label: Grid connection
lanes.note: Almost always the longest path. Start it first.
lanes.levelNote: Provincial system operator and a regulated utility. The municipality is a stakeholder here, not the decision-maker.

lanes.label: Utilities regulator
lanes.note: Approves the substation and any on-site generation — not the building.
lanes.levelNote: Provincial quasi-judicial regulator. Its decisions are made under provincial statute, not the land use bylaw.

lanes.label: Environment & water
lanes.note: Independent of the land use decision, and can be the quiet blocker.
lanes.levelNote: Provincial department. Independent of the municipal land use decision.

lanes.label: Municipal
lanes.note: Land use, servicing, and the conditions you can actually enforce.
lanes.levelNote: Your authority. Council and the development authority, under the Municipal Government Act.

lanes.label: Building & safety
lanes.note: Follows the development permit and ends at occupancy.
lanes.levelNote: Provincial statute, usually administered municipally: the Safety Codes Act is provincial, but most municipalities are accredited to issue and inspect. Confirm who is accredited in your jurisdiction — it is not the same everywhere.

nodes.title: System access service request
nodes.what: Ask AESO for transmission system access. This opens the queue position that everything downstream depends on.
nodes.why: The single longest lead item on the project, and the one most often started too late. A queue position obtained in month one is worth more than any amount of expediting later.

nodes.title: System study & connection proposal
nodes.what: AESO and the transmission facility owner determine the point of interconnection, the substation required, and any system reinforcement.
nodes.why: This output defines the substation footprint, which the municipal site plan has to accommodate. Getting it before the development permit is drawn saves a redesign.

nodes.title: Connection agreement & cost commitment
nodes.what: The proponent accepts the connection proposal, enters the system access service agreement with AESO, and posts the security and construction contribution that lets the transmission facility owner begin work.
nodes.why: This is where a grid connection stops being an enquiry and becomes a commitment. Until it is signed and secured, a queue position is not a connection — an application that presents an AESO study as though it were an approval is overstating what it holds. Ask what has actually been executed. In the same phase, and separately, the AUC decides the substation itself.
nodes.watch: Confirm the current instrument name and the security terms against the AESO tariff before relying on them — the sequence is stable, the naming has changed before.

nodes.title: Substation construction
nodes.what: The transmission facility owner builds the substation and connection, under the AUC permit and against the executed connection agreement, on the grid’s schedule.
nodes.why: Two things gate this, not one: the AUC permit for the facility and the proponent’s executed commitment to AESO. Either one outstanding stops the build, which is why both arrows converge here.

nodes.title: Energization
nodes.what: Power is available at the site.
nodes.why: A finished building with no firm connection is a stranded asset. Tying occupancy — not construction — to evidence of energization is enforceable and within municipal jurisdiction.

nodes.title: Participant involvement programme
nodes.what: Notification and consultation with landowners and occupants within the rule's radius, before the facility application is filed.
nodes.why: Ask to be included. The AUC's notification radius and the municipality's differ, and residents notified by one process and not the other is the most common source of 'nobody told us' at a public hearing.

nodes.title: Facility application
nodes.what: Application for the substation, with the noise assessment required by the Commission's noise rule. A power plant on the same site is a separate application — see the generation chain below.
nodes.why: The noise study filed here is usually the only acoustic modelling in existence before the municipality has to decide. Read it.

nodes.title: Permit & licence
nodes.what: The Commission decides, and attaches its own conditions on siting, noise and reclamation.
nodes.why: Compare these conditions with your draft conditions. Where the AUC has imposed a stricter limit, adopt it by reference rather than writing a weaker parallel one.

nodes.title: Water Act licence or approval
nodes.what: Required where the project draws groundwater or surface water rather than a municipal supply.
nodes.why: A permit granted against an unlicensed supply is not deliverable. Ask whether a licence or transfer is in hand and whether its volume matches the stated use.

nodes.title: Environmental & historical clearances
nodes.what: Wetland assessment, environmental approvals where thresholds are engaged, and Historical Resources Act clearance.
nodes.why: These are independent of the land use decision and run on their own timetable. They rarely stop a project, but they routinely delay one.

nodes.title: Pre-application meeting
nodes.what: Confirm the land use district, whether the use is permitted or discretionary, servicing capacity, and whether a statutory plan amendment is needed.
nodes.why: Municipal leverage is at its highest here and falls steadily afterwards. Establish the ultimate build-out load, not the first phase, and get it in writing.

nodes.title: Redesignation or plan amendment
nodes.what: Land use bylaw amendment, and any area structure plan amendment, where the current designation does not accommodate the use.
nodes.why: Only some projects need this. Where it is needed it adds a council process and a public hearing, and it is the point at which the community has a statutory voice.

nodes.title: Development permit application
nodes.what: The formal application, circulation and referrals.
nodes.why: Decide here whether the substation forms part of this application or a separate provincial one, and say so in writing. The substation is approved by the AUC; this permit is not that approval.

nodes.title: Decision & development agreement
nodes.what: The permit decision with conditions, and the agreement fixing servicing, off-site levies, road use and security.
nodes.why: The agreement outlasts the permit and is the most durable instrument the municipality holds. Cost recovery is secured here or not at all.

nodes.title: Site grading
nodes.what: Stripping and earthworks, often begun before the building permit issues.
nodes.why: Once a large site is stripped, refusing what follows becomes far harder to defend. Require security sized to actual reclamation cost and a drainage design that works as a standalone end state.

nodes.title: Building & trade permits
nodes.what: Building permit, then electrical, plumbing and gas permits under the Safety Codes Act.

nodes.title: Inspections
nodes.what: Staged inspections through construction.

nodes.title: Occupancy permit
nodes.what: Legal occupation of the building.
nodes.why: Three separate authorities have to be satisfied before this issues. The grid connection is the one most likely to be outstanding.

nodes.title: Power plant application
nodes.what: A separate application under the Hydro and Electric Energy Act where the project proposes on-site generation, including gas-fired plant serving the load.
nodes.why: This is a different application from the substation, with its own record, its own noise and emissions case, and often its own hearing. A project can win one and lose the other — as the Olds decision showed.

nodes.title: Power plant approval & licence
nodes.what: The Commission's decision on the generating facility, with its own conditions on siting, noise, emissions and reclamation.
nodes.why: Approval here authorises the generating facility. It does not authorise the buildings, access, or site development around it — those remain municipal, which is why the paired municipal permit exists.

nodes.title: Development permit — generation facility
nodes.what: The municipal permit for the generating facility and its site works, separate from the data centre's own development permit.
nodes.why: An AUC approval for a power plant does not remove the municipal approvals that go with building it — the site development, access and associated works still come to you. Treat it as its own file with its own conditions, not as a footnote to the data centre permit.
nodes.watch: How a provincial approval interacts with municipal land use authority is addressed in the Municipal Government Act, and the effect is fact-specific. Confirm the current position with your solicitor before concluding what you can and cannot condition.

insights.title: The grid is the critical path
insights.text: Every other approval can usually be obtained faster than a transmission connection. If the AESO request has not been made, the project timeline in the application is unsupported — regardless of how advanced the design is.

insights.title: The grid track does not stop at the study
insights.text: The system study is the middle of the grid path, not the end of it. What follows is the connection agreement and cost commitment, the AUC’s decision on the substation, construction by the transmission facility owner, and finally energization — which is what occupancy should be conditioned on.

insights.title: Four things should start in week one
insights.text: The AESO request, the municipal pre-application, any water licence, and the AUC participant involvement programme are all independent of each other. Running them in sequence rather than in parallel adds months for no reason.

insights.title: A power plant needs both approvals
insights.text: Where a project proposes on-site generation, the AUC approves the generating facility and the municipality still permits the site development around it. They are separate files on separate records, and the pairing is shown by the dashed links. Neither one authorises the other.

insights.title: Two approvals, one site
insights.text: The municipality approves the building; the AUC approves the substation that powers it. Neither authorises the other, and both site plans must show the same footprint — reconcile them at pre-application, not at decision.

insights.title: Occupancy is the real gate
insights.text: Construction can finish while the connection is still outstanding. Conditioning occupancy — rather than construction — on evidence of a firm connection is enforceable, within municipal jurisdiction, and prevents a stranded building.

levels.label: Provincial
levels.note: Decided under provincial statute. You are consulted, not deciding.

levels.label: Municipal
levels.note: Decided by council or the development authority under the MGA.

levels.label: Provincial statute, municipal administration
levels.note: Provincial rules, usually applied by an accredited municipality.
